summary: The note is a Wikipedia article describing the fog bow, a rainbow-like optical phenomenon formed by fog droplets rather than rain. It explains that fog bows are very weakly colored or white because the droplets are tiny, distinguishes them from glories, and notes related terms such as cloud bow, sea-dog and lunar fog bow. It also lists see-also links and references.
one_line: A fog bow is a weakly colored, rainbow-like optical phenomenon formed by tiny fog droplets rather than rain.
key_facts: A fog bow is a phenomenon similar to a rainbow that appears as a bow in fog rather than rain.
A fog bow is sometimes called a white rainbow.
The water droplets that cause fog are smaller than 0.05 millimeters (0.0020 in).
Fog bows have only very weak colors, with a red outer edge and bluish inner edge.
The colors of a fog bow fade because they are smeared out by the diffraction effect of the smaller droplets.
Fog bows appear white when the droplets are very small, which distinguishes them from a glory.
When droplets forming a fog bow are almost all the same size, the bow can have multiple inner rings called supernumeraries, which are more strongly colored than the main bow.
A fog bow seen in clouds, typically from an aircraft looking downwards, is called a cloud bow.
Mariners sometimes call fog bows sea-dogs.
A fog bow is seen in the same direction as a rainbow, with the sun behind the observer's head.
The outer radius of a fog bow is slightly less than that of a rainbow.
A fog bow seen at night is called a lunar fog bow.
The article's references include Auguste Bravais's 1847 paper 'Sur le phénomène de l'arc-en-ciel blanc' and James C. McConnel's 1890 paper 'The theory of fog-bows'.
